numberItems.stem: Which list shows the handbook's basic steps at an accident, in order?
options: Care for the injured, protect the area, notify authorities, collect information, report
Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured, collect information, report
Notify authorities, collect information, protect the area, care for the injured, report
numberItems.explanation: The basic steps are: protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured, collect required information, and report the accident. Preventing a second crash comes first (p. 2-44).

numberItems.stem: A person hurt in a crash is bleeding heavily and no one qualified is there. What should you do?
options: Apply direct pressure to the wound
Move them to the shoulder first
Give them water and keep them walking
numberItems.explanation: Stop heavy bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound, and keep the injured person warm; don't move a badly injured person unless fire or traffic makes it necessary (p. 2-44).

numberItems.stem: Name two causes of tire fires.
options: Over-inflated tires and worn tread
Driver smoking and loose fuel connections
Under-inflated tires and dual tires that touch
numberItems.explanation: Tire fires are caused by under-inflated tires and dual tires that touch. Smoking and loose fuel connections are fuel-fire causes (p. 2-44).

numberItems.stem: During a trip, what does the handbook say to check for signs of heat every time you stop?
options: Only the engine oil level
The tires, wheels, and truck body
Only the cargo doors
numberItems.explanation: En route inspection: check the tires, wheels, and truck body for signs of heat whenever you stop during a trip (p. 2-44).

numberItems.stem: You are about to use a fire extinguisher. Where should you stand?
options: As close to the fire as you can, downwind
As far from the fire as possible, upwind
Close to the fire, upwind
numberItems.explanation: Stay as far away from the fire as possible and position yourself upwind so the wind carries the extinguisher to the fire (p. 2-45).

numberItems.stem: Where should you aim a fire extinguisher?
options: At the source or base of the fire
Up in the flames
Into the smoke
numberItems.explanation: Aim at the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames (p. 2-45).

numberItems.stem: An A:B:C fire extinguisher is designed to work on:
options: Burning metals only
Burning wood, paper, and cloth only
Electrical fires and burning liquids, and also burning wood, paper, and cloth
numberItems.explanation: The B:C type works on electrical fires and burning liquids; the A:B:C type also works on burning wood, paper, and cloth (p. 2-45).

numberItems.stem: Why should you never use water on a **gasoline** fire?
options: It will spread the flames
It can give you an electric shock
It cools the fire too slowly to help
numberItems.explanation: Water on a gasoline fire will spread the flames; on an electrical fire it can cause shock (p. 2-45).

numberItems.stem: One of your tires is on fire. What does the handbook say?
options: Never use water on a burning tire
It must be cooled, and it may take lots of water
Pull into the nearest service station for help
numberItems.explanation: A burning tire must be cooled; lots of water may be required. Never pull into a service station (p. 2-45).

numberItems.stem: A fire in electrical equipment is which class of fire?
options: Class B
Class D
Class C
numberItems.explanation: Class C fires are electrical-equipment fires (no water). Class B is gasoline, oil, grease; Class D is burning metals (p. 2-45).

numberItems.stem: Under the on-duty rules, you may not drink any intoxicating beverage, no matter how weak, within how many hours before going on duty?
options: 8 hours
2 hours
4 hours
numberItems.explanation: You may never drink on duty or consume any intoxicating beverage, regardless of alcohol content, within 4 hours before going on duty (p. 2-46).

numberItems.stem: Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is measured in milligrams of alcohol per how much blood?
options: 100 milliliters
1,000 milliliters
12 ounces
numberItems.explanation: BAC is the amount of alcohol recorded in milligrams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood (p. 2-46).

numberItems.stem: A BAC of .10 means:
options: 10% of your blood is alcohol
1/10 of 1% (1/1000) of your blood is alcohol
1% of your blood is alcohol
numberItems.explanation: A BAC of .10 means that 1/10 of 1% (or 1/1000) of your total blood content is alcohol (p. 2-46).

numberItems.stem: [CA] A CMV driver is stopped with a BAC of .05. Which is true?
options: It is legal, because the limit is .08
It is legal, because the limit is .10
It is illegal — driving a CMV at 0.04% or more is against the law
numberItems.explanation: It is illegal to drive a CMV with a BAC of 0.04% or greater (CVC §13353.2, §23152(d); p. 2-47). The .08 figure on the chart is not the CMV limit.

numberItems.stem: About how much **pure alcohol** can the liver process per hour?
options: About 1/10 ounce
About 1/3 ounce
About 5 ounces
numberItems.explanation: The liver can only process about 1/3 ounce of alcohol per hour, a fixed rate — only time sobers you up (p. 2-47).

numberItems.stem: When using the handbook's BAC chart (Figure 2.22), how much do you subtract for the time spent drinking?
options: .01% for each 40 minutes
.04% for each 40 minutes
.01% for each 4 hours
numberItems.explanation: The chart says to subtract .01% for each 40 minutes of drinking (p. 2-46).

numberItems.stem: Which drink has the same amount of alcohol as a 12-ounce glass of 5% beer?
options: A 12-ounce glass of 12% wine
A 5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor
A 5-ounce glass of 12% wine
numberItems.explanation: A 12-oz glass of 5% beer, a 5-oz glass of 12% wine, and a 1½-oz shot of 80-proof liquor all contain the same amount of alcohol (p. 2-47).

numberItems.stem: What three things determine your blood alcohol concentration?
options: How much you drink, how fast you drink, and your weight
Whether you drink beer or liquor, your height, and the time of day
How much you drink, whether you drink coffee, and your weight
numberItems.explanation: BAC is determined by the amount of alcohol you drink, how fast you drink, and your weight (p. 2-47). The type of drink doesn't matter and coffee doesn't lower BAC.

numberItems.stem: As BAC builds up, which brain function is affected **first**?
options: Muscle control
Judgment and self-control
Vision
numberItems.explanation: The first part of the brain affected controls judgment and self-control; muscle control, vision and coordination are affected as BAC keeps building (p. 2-47).

numberItems.stem: According to the handbook, what is the only cure for fatigue?
options: A drug that keeps you awake
Coffee and fresh air
Rest
numberItems.explanation: Do not use any drug that hides fatigue — the only cure for fatigue is rest (p. 2-47).

numberItems.stem: The HazMat rules are meant to do which three things?
options: Contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment
Contain the product, lower shipping costs, and speed up deliveries
Placard every load, avoid cities, and ship only at night
numberItems.explanation: The intent of the HazMat rules is to contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment (p. 2-48).

numberItems.stem: While you are driving, where may you keep HazMat shipping papers?
options: Locked in the glove box
In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach
Under the other shipping papers in the sleeper
numberItems.explanation: Keep HazMat shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's door or in clear view within reach while driving, and on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle (p. 2-48).

numberItems.stem: Your load requires placards. Which placarding is correct?
options: 2 placards — front and rear
1 placard on each side
At least 4 identical placards — front, rear, and both sides
numberItems.explanation: A placarded vehicle must have at least 4 identical placards on the front, rear, and both sides, readable from all 4 directions (p. 2-48).

numberItems.stem: According to this handbook, how big must a HazMat placard be?
options: At least 10¾ inches square, turned upright on a point
At least 9.84 inches (250 mm) square, turned upright on a point
At least 12 inches square, turned upright on a point
numberItems.explanation: Placards must be at least 9.84 inches (250 mm) square, turned upright on a point in a diamond shape. Some older sources say 10¾ inches (p. 2-48).

numberItems.stem: How many digits does a HazMat ID number have?
numberItems.explanation: ID numbers are a 4-digit code, preceded by the letters "UN" or "NA" (p. 2-48).

numberItems.stem: First responders want to look up the chemical behind a HazMat ID number. Which book lists chemicals and their ID numbers?
options: The FMCSA driver's logbook
The U.S. DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
The vehicle owner's manual
numberItems.explanation: The U.S. DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) lists the chemicals and the ID numbers assigned to them (p. 2-48).

numberItems.stem: When do you need an "H" endorsement to drive a vehicle carrying HazMat?
options: Whenever the load contains any HazMat at all
Only when the HazMat is in a cargo tank
When the load requires placards
numberItems.explanation: You can drive a vehicle carrying HazMat if it does not require placards; if it requires placards, you need the "H" endorsement (p. 2-49).

numberItems.stem: A CMV hauling liquid in tanks counts as a tank vehicle when:
options: Each tank holds more than 119 gallons and all tanks together hold 1,000 gallons or more
Each tank holds more than 1,000 gallons and all tanks together hold 119 gallons or more
Any single tank holds 119 gallons or more, whatever the total
numberItems.explanation: The tank endorsement applies to tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more (p. 2-49).
